image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Point map / geospatial dot distribution map** of the continental United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses a **single map panel** (no faceting or small multiples).
- Points are **overlaid** on a U.S. basemap with **state boundaries and state labels**.
- No stacking is used.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (longitude) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on horizontal map axis |
| Geographic location (latitude) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on vertical map axis |
| Individual observation / event presence | Categorical / nominal (record presence) | Small red point marks |
| State / state name | Categorical / nominal | Text labels on map |
| State boundaries | Categorical / nominal geographic regions | Light gray boundary lines |

If you want, I can also provide this in a stricter computer-vision annotation style.

Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of these graphs:  "Land Being Developed the United States. Where and Why?" by Elizabeth of Iowa and “Everyone's Headed East: Land Development Shows an Increase in the East and Barely Any in the West.” By Kerry of Chicago and "Spreading Out: New Land Development in the US" by Kaitlin of Massachusetts.

 

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, March 19 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the map, and a few Stat Nuggets.

 

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).

View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 

graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 

Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex). 

 

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, whose city’s Seaport District is featured in the article, and Greg Yarnall of Morristown, New Jersey, who promises that there are undeveloped parts of the Garden State of NJ.

comments.raw_comment: After analyzing the graph, our group noticed several things such as the East and South Coast have more land development than the West Coast. We also noticed that Texas has the largest red dots in a cluster, while states like Nevada, Wyoming, Montana, South Dakota, Oregon, and Nebraska, have had less land development over the years. In addition, we noticed that the population of a city does not really coincide with the new development in certain areas in the United States. The last thing we noticed was that some clusters of land development made a circular shape around the city that they were in. After making observations, our group had some questions about the graph like why there is more development in the East compared to the West. Another thing we wondered was what kind of land development they are referring to, public business areas or more private residential areas. We also wondered why Texas had so many concentrated areas of red dots. This impacts our community positively because the more developed a location has, the more opportunities for people and the more people come there to visit which grows that location a lot. Lastly, this impacts our community negatively because it means that forests and trees could be destroyed to make room for new development such as apartment buildings, houses, or roads. A catchy headline for this graph is “New Development in the United States."

comments.raw_comment:
Sprawling across America: The increasing size of our cities
We notice that new land has developed a lot where there are big cities and a large population. Also, the east coast tends to have more development than the rest of the country. The midwest has the least amount of development. Oregon looks like it has the least amount of development. Although Connecticut is small it does look like it has the most development. Texas development is very condensed in some areas but in the rest very condensed. Most states have either very condensed areas only in certain spots or are not very condensed but have small spots all over. We wonder how much more previously natural we have destroyed before 2008. I wonder why there is more land development in smaller states rather than larger ones. This impacts us in many ways, for example, since this map shows how urban sprawl is leading to increasingly large metropolitan areas, this could negatively impact our community by getting rid of wildlife areas and replacing them with man-made structures.

comments.raw_comment: In the data provided by the graph, our group found several things that caught our interest. First, we noticed much of the new development has taken place around major cities. While the urban areas in cities remain the same, developments are created in suburban areas surrounding the cities. A lot of new developments have occurred in some of the most populated states, such as Texas, California, and Florida. We also noticed that many of the new developments are concentrated in one specific area rather than being spread throughout a state. In Minnesota, the development was centered around the Twin Cities - we wonder if most of the development in other states are around major cities as well? Additionally, what is going around in the western area of North Dakota and why is so much development taking place there? We also found that there was not a lot of recent development in Maine? Are property taxes too high? What would cause private or public contractors to build elsewhere? Based on these new developments, this impacts both us and our community as new development is important for creating opportunities and providing for an expanding population. As development continues across the country, it is important that investments are made in states where new infrastructure is direly needed. We would title this headline, “As the U.S. Population Expands, so do the Nation’s Cities.”

comments.raw_comment: This graph shows the amount of new land development across the continental United States. Based on the graph, our group noticed that there seems to be a fair bit more development on the eastern side of the United States. The west has only a few regions with a lot of development, and there is a fair bit of empty area. Our group was surprised with how much area lacked any new development throughout the entire country. Our group wonders about the effectiveness of this graph and others like it. The areas of density on these types of maps are all generally quite similar to a population map. Comparing this map to a population map you can pinpoint all the big cities and densely populated places in the same areas where new development is occurring. More people will simply increase the number of data points in that area. Despite this graphs like these still have a purpose for the community. For one it allows us where new construction would be likely to occur, which may affect our interest in moving to a particular area.

Title: Which states are developing the fastest? 
We notice that a lot of new land development happens around big cities. There is a large area of the east coast that has a lot of new land development. We also notice that the land development areas tend to be really condensed in one area. One state with lots of land development is Texas.
We wonder why the east seems to have more new land development vs the west and why are some of the newer land developments even necessary…? Also, we wonder if maybe there might be a relation between the number of people who develop new land and the population of people in the United States? The impact that we are seeing is that many suburbs are being developed right now. There are a lot of rings on this map, and that shows that inner city land is not being developed right now. Instead, there is a ton of work being done in the suburbs. Expanding metropolitan areas are very common right now as shown in this graph.

comments.raw_comment: I notice that this is a map which tells us where new land has developed in the continental Untied States in the past decade. The blotches of red are areas where land was developed for homes, commercial centers, large buildings, and other facilities. I also notice that there is less land development in the west while there is more in the east. I wonder as to why is it that we see more land development in the east and not the west. This is because the west is notorious for having so much space and less developed land, so I would like to know why there is more development in the east if this area is already pretty condensed and immensely developed. This impacts my community in the sense that I live in the Northeast, and I worry that there will be too much development in my area. With land development comes more people, so it makes me a little anxious that my community may become very overpopulated. I know that in California, specifically L.A, there already is a lot of people there and the air quality is not  so healthy. Hopefully the same does not happen here. Potential catchy headline: "How Does Land Development Impact Your Future?"
